lesson.title: First Come, First Served: Lists as Queues
lesson.summary: A queue processes items in the order they arrived, first in first out, but building one naively out of a plain list is quietly slow, which is exactly why Python provides collections.deque for the job.
lesson.body:
A queue is the mirror image of a stack: instead of last in, first out, it is first in, first out, or FIFO. Think of a line at a store: whoever arrived first gets served first. If you tried to build a queue using only the list operations from the stack pattern, you would append to add new items to the back, which is fine, but you would need pop(0) to remove from the front, since that is where the oldest item sits.

```python
queue = []
queue.append('first')
queue.append('second')
queue.append('third')
print(queue.pop(0))
print(queue)
```

This prints 'first', the item that was enqueued earliest, followed by ['second', 'third']. Functionally, this works. The problem is performance, and it is worth understanding exactly why. A Python list stores its elements in one contiguous block of memory, indexed by position. When you call pop(0), Python removes the element at index 0, but then it must also shift every single remaining element one position to the left, so that index 1 becomes index 0, index 2 becomes index 1, and so on. For a list of n elements, that shifting takes O(n) time, not the O(1) time you get from popping off the end of a list, as you saw with stacks. The same problem applies to insert(0, value) if you tried to enqueue at the front instead: it also has to shift every existing element to make room. A queue built this way gets slower and slower as it grows, which is a real problem if your program processes thousands of items.

The fix is to use collections.deque, short for double-ended queue, a data structure the Python standard library provides specifically because plain lists are the wrong tool for this job. A deque supports appendleft and popleft in addition to append and pop, and all four operations run in O(1) time, because a deque is implemented internally so that adding or removing from either end never requires shifting the other elements.

```python
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
queue.append('first')
queue.append('second')
queue.append('third')
print(queue)
print(queue.popleft())
print(queue)
```

This prints deque(['first', 'second', 'third']), then 'first', the oldest item, then deque(['second', 'third']). The pattern is the mirror of the stack: enqueue with append on one end, dequeue with popleft on the other. The general rule to remember is this: for a stack, where you only ever add and remove from one end, a plain list is perfectly efficient. For a real queue, where you regularly remove from the front, prefer collections.deque over a plain list, because pop(0) on a list is O(n) while popleft() on a deque is O(1).
